title: Water, Weak Bonds, and the Generation of Order

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Protein folding creates order. Why does it not violate the second law of thermodynamics?
cards.back: The second law concerns total entropy: the protein, its water, and the surroundings that exchange heat with them. At constant T and P that total rises whenever ΔG for protein-plus-water is negative.
cards.why: Heat released raises the surroundings' entropy by −ΔH/T, so the total entropy change is ΔS − ΔH/T = −ΔG/T.
cards.quote: The second law is about the total: the protein, its water, and the heat they exchange with everything else.

cards.front: A change goes forward when the free energy of the molecule plus its water falls ({{c1::ΔG < 0}}).
cards.back: Count the water, not just the molecule.
cards.quote: A change goes forward when the free energy of the molecule plus its water falls (ΔG < 0).

cards.front: What is RT at 37 °C, and how many RT is one weak interaction worth in water?
cards.back: RT ≈ 2.6 kJ/mol at 37 °C. A weak interaction in water is worth only about one to a few RT net, so no single contact decides anything; the sum decides.
cards.quote: In water, each weak interaction is worth only about one to a few RT net

cards.front: One pH unit changes the free energy of a group's protonation by 2.303 RT. Taking RT ≈ 2.6 kJ/mol at 37 °C, how large is that, and how does it compare with a weak bond?
cards.back: 2.303 × 2.6 ≈ 5.9 to 6 kJ/mol, about the size of one weak bond. A shift of one pH unit is one more weak-bond-sized term in the ledger.
cards.quote: one pH unit changes the free energy of a group's protonation by 2.303 RT, about 5.9 kJ/mol, the size of one weak bond

cards.front: Why is a water molecule an electric dipole?
cards.back: Oxygen pulls electrons far harder than hydrogen, so O is partly negative and each H partly positive. The molecule is bent (about 104.5°), so the partial charges do not cancel.
cards.quote: The molecule bends at about 104.5 degrees, so those charges don't cancel: water is an electric dipole
cards.section: Water is the engine, not the stage

cards.front: Name the three jobs water's polarity gives it in the cell.
cards.back: It sticks to itself (a hydrogen-bonded network), it dissolves many charged things, and it rejects anything nonpolar.
cards.quote: It sticks to itself, hydrogen end to oxygen end, in a flickering network
cards.section: Water is the engine, not the stage

cards.front: In liquid water's hydrogen-bond network, each bond forms and breaks in a few {{c1::trillionths of a second}}.
cards.quote: each bond forms and breaks in a few trillionths of a second
cards.section: Water is the engine, not the stage

cards.front: A K⁺ ion and a negatively charged phosphate group are each dissolved in water. Which atom of the surrounding water molecules faces each one, and why?
cards.back: Water's oxygens face K⁺; water's hydrogens face the phosphate. The partly negative O is drawn to the cation and the partly positive H to the anion, as with Na⁺ and Cl⁻.
cards.quote: wrapping a sodium ion in a shell of oxygens and a chloride in a shell of hydrogens
cards.section: Water is the engine, not the stage

cards.front: Why does the cell rely on weak, breakable bonds rather than covalent bonds for binding events such as odorant to receptor?
cards.back: Reversibility is the point: the ligand must bind, trigger a signal, and fall off. Covalent binding would make the signal permanent.
cards.quote: If that binding were covalent, you would smell that cat for the rest of your life.
cards.section: Weak on purpose, measured in RT

cards.front: Measured in RT, why does thermal jostling almost never break a covalent bond but constantly breaks weak bonds?
cards.back: Covalent bonds are about 40 to 400 RT, far above thermal energy. A bond worth one or two RT breaks and re-forms all the time.
cards.quote: covalent bonds are about 40 to 400 RT, so heat almost never breaks them
cards.section: Weak on purpose, measured in RT

cards.front: What are the donor and the acceptor in a hydrogen bond?
cards.back: Donor: a hydrogen bonded to a strongly electronegative atom, O or N. Acceptor: a lone pair on another O or N.
cards.quote: a hydrogen on a strongly electronegative atom, O or N (the donor), is drawn to a lone pair on another O or N
cards.section: Hydrogen bonds: who can donate

cards.front: Why can a methyl group (–CH₃) neither donate nor accept a useful hydrogen bond?
cards.back: Carbon's electronegativity (2.55) is too close to hydrogen's (2.20) to leave the H much positive charge, and the methyl carbon has no lone pair. So methyl groups are nonpolar.
cards.quote: carbon's electronegativity (2.55) is too close to hydrogen's (2.20) to leave the hydrogen much positive charge
cards.section: Hydrogen bonds: who can donate

cards.front: Classify each as H-bond donor, acceptor, both, or neither: threonine's –OH, a backbone carbonyl oxygen (C=O), and leucine's hydrocarbon side chain.
cards.back: Threonine –OH: both (H on O, plus O lone pairs). Carbonyl O: acceptor only (lone pairs, no attached H). Leucine side chain: neither (only C–H).
cards.why: Donor needs H on O or N; acceptor needs a lone pair on O or N.
cards.quote: and the methyl carbon has no lone pair to accept one
cards.section: Hydrogen bonds: who can donate

cards.front: A hydrogen bond is worth about 10 to 40 kJ/mol in a vacuum. Why is its net gain in water only a few kJ/mol?
cards.back: The donor and acceptor were already hydrogen-bonded to water, so pairing them mostly trades one bond for another. The net gain is one to a few RT.
cards.quote: In water the donor and acceptor were already hydrogen-bonded to water, so pairing them mostly trades one bond for another
cards.section: Hydrogen bonds: who can donate

cards.front: In Coulomb's law, E = kq₁q₂/(Dr), what is D, and what are its approximate values for a vacuum, water, and a protein interior?
cards.back: D is the dielectric constant, how well the medium screens charge: 1 for a vacuum, about 80 for water, about 2 to 4 inside a protein.
cards.quote: 1 for a vacuum, about 80 for water, about 2 to 4 inside a protein
cards.section: Charges: why water evens things out

cards.front: Two opposite charges 4 Å apart attract with about 350 kJ/mol in a vacuum. Estimate the attraction at the same distance inside a protein (D ≈ 4) and in water (D ≈ 80).
cards.back: E scales as 1/D. Protein: 350 / 4 ≈ 90 kJ/mol. Water: 350 / 80 ≈ 4 kJ/mol.
cards.quote: Two opposite charges 4 Å apart attract with about 350 kJ/mol in a vacuum
cards.section: Charges: why water evens things out

cards.front: Rank ionic, hydrogen-bond and van der Waals interactions in a vacuum. How does the ranking change in water?
cards.back: Vacuum: ionic > hydrogen bond > van der Waals. In water an exposed salt bridge gets at most about 4 to 6 kJ/mol from Coulomb's law, no stronger than a hydrogen bond's net share.
cards.why: Water's high dielectric constant screens charges, so it evens the interactions out.
cards.quote: So in a vacuum, ionic beats hydrogen bond beats van der Waals
cards.section: Charges: why water evens things out

cards.front: A glutamate–lysine salt bridge moves from the protein surface (D ≈ 80) into the core (D ≈ 3) at the same distance. Does the protein gain the full Coulombic increase in stability?
cards.back: No. Coulomb's law alone gives about 27-fold stronger attraction (80/3), but both charges must shed their water to enter the core. That desolvation penalty can cost as much as the attraction gains.
cards.why: The net effect ranges from destabilizing to several kcal/mol.
cards.quote: that desolvation penalty can cost as much as the attraction gains
cards.section: Charges: why water evens things out

cards.front: Adding ethanol to a salty aqueous DNA solution makes the DNA clump into a white thread. Which physical law explains this, and how?
cards.back: Coulomb's law: ethanol lowers the dielectric constant D, so attraction between the negative phosphates and counterions such as Na⁺ strengthens and the DNA aggregates.
cards.quote: Ethanol lowers D, the attraction between the negative phosphates and counterions such as sodium strengthens
cards.section: Charges: why water evens things out

cards.front: A surface glutamate–lysine salt bridge stabilizes a protein. The pH is lowered well below the glutamate side chain's pKa. Predict what happens to the salt bridge, and why.
cards.back: It is largely lost. Below its pKa the glutamate mostly holds its proton, so it is mostly neutral and has little charge for the lysine to attract.
cards.why: pH sets which groups carry charge; Coulombic attraction needs two charges.
cards.quote: Ionic attractions, and many hydrogen bonds, depend on whether a group is charged, which depends on pH.
cards.section: pH: the ledger for charge

cards.front: Hydrogen bonds and van der Waals contacts work at roughly {{c1::three to four Ångströms}} between atoms; closer, atoms repel, and a little farther the attraction fades fast.
cards.back: Ionic attraction reaches farther, though water and salt damp it.
cards.quote: roughly three to four Ångströms (a few ten-billionths of a meter) between atoms
cards.section: The four-Ångström window

cards.front: A single van der Waals contact is worth under about 4 kJ/mol. Why can many such contacts together give very tight, specific binding?
cards.back: The energies add, and because an equilibrium constant grows exponentially with energy, their effects on binding multiply.
cards.why: A gecko hangs from a ceiling mainly on van der Waals forces made by the many branching hairs on its feet.
cards.quote: since an equilibrium constant grows exponentially with energy, their effects multiply
cards.section: The four-Ångström window

cards.front: Using K = e^(ΔE/RT) with RT ≈ 2.6 kJ/mol, estimate the equilibrium constant contributed by one 4 kJ/mol contact and by ten such contacts acting together.
cards.back: One: e^(4/2.6) ≈ e^1.5 ≈ 5. Ten: e^(40/2.6) ≈ e^15.4 ≈ 5 million. This is an upper bound; in water the net gain per contact is smaller.
cards.quote: one 4 kJ/mol contact gives a constant of about 5, ten acting together about 5 million
cards.section: The four-Ångström window

cards.front: Why does the layer of water next to a nonpolar group such as a methyl have lower entropy than bulk water?
cards.back: Water cannot hydrogen-bond to the methyl, so it keeps its hydrogen bonds by pointing them along the surface toward other water. That layer has fewer possible arrangements.
cards.why: It is a slightly stiffer layer, only modestly more ordered than bulk, not a rigid cage.
cards.quote: That first layer has fewer ways to arrange itself than bulk water: lower entropy.
cards.section: What pays for order: the hydrophobic effect

cards.front: A protein chain folds and buries its nonpolar side chains. Predict the sign of ΔS for the chain and for the water, and explain each.
cards.back: Chain: negative, because a floppy chain with an astronomical number of shapes is held in roughly one. Water: positive, because water that lined the buried surface is released into the bulk.
cards.quote: The chain's entropy falls: a floppy chain that could take an astronomical number of shapes is held in roughly one.
cards.section: What pays for order: the hydrophobic effect

cards.front: What is the hydrophobic effect, and why do nonpolar groups end up together in water?
cards.back: It is the release of surface-lining water when nonpolar groups gather. They cluster mainly because gathering shrinks the surface water must line, not because they attract each other.
cards.why: Near room temperature the gain is almost all entropy; enthalpy's share grows with temperature and at large flat surfaces.
cards.quote: Nonpolar groups end up together mainly because gathering them shrinks the surface water has to line, not because they attract each other
cards.section: What pays for order: the hydrophobic effect

cards.front: For folding a protein of about 100 residues near 25 °C, give the rough ledger (kJ/mol; positive opposes folding).
cards.back: Chain loses freedom of shape: about +550. Water freed from buried nonpolar surface: about −500. Net hydrogen bonds, ion pairs and packing: about −90. ΔG of folding: about −40.
cards.why: The third row is a remainder; measured ΔG for small proteins is about −20 to −60 kJ/mol.
cards.quote: Here is the account for folding a protein of about 100 residues near 25 °C, in round numbers
cards.section: What pays for order: the hydrophobic effect

cards.front: Using the rule of thumb of about 25 cal/mol per Å² of nonpolar surface buried, estimate the favorable term from burying 4,800 Å² in kJ/mol.
cards.back: 4,800 × 25 cal = 120,000 cal = 120 kcal ≈ 500 kJ/mol favoring folding.
cards.quote: about 25 cal/mol for each Å² of nonpolar surface buried (4,800 × 25 cal is about 500 kJ)
cards.section: What pays for order: the hydrophobic effect

cards.front: Near 25 °C the water's entropy gain in folding (about −480 kJ/mol as −TΔS) is smaller than the chain's entropy loss (about +550). How can folding still raise the entropy of everything?
cards.back: Chain plus water lose a little entropy, but bonds and packing release heat as they form, raising the surroundings' entropy. Overall ΔG is negative, so total entropy rises.
cards.why: Rests on ΔS_total = −ΔG/T from the opening ledger rule.
cards.quote: So the chain plus its water lose a little entropy, and the rest is paid in heat
cards.section: What pays for order: the hydrophobic effect

cards.front: A protein folds with ΔG ≈ −40 kJ/mol, and its hydrophobic burial term is about −500 kJ/mol. A mutation reduces burial by 10%. Predict the folding outcome.
cards.back: 10% of 500 is 50 kJ/mol, so in these round numbers ΔG shifts from about −40 to about +10: the 50 kJ/mol shift is larger than the 40 kJ/mol margin, so folding is no longer favored in this ledger.
cards.why: Folding stability is a small difference between big numbers, so proteins are only modestly stable.
cards.quote: change the burial row by 10% (50 of its 500) and the total moves by 50 kJ/mol, more than the total itself
cards.section: What pays for order: the hydrophobic effect

cards.front: Why do phospholipids form a closed bilayer rather than micelles, and what holds the bilayer together?
cards.back: With two greasy tails a phospholipid is too bulky to pack into a micelle, so it forms a tail-to-tail sheet that closes to leave no tails exposed at an edge. Water's entropy, not any enzyme, holds it together.
cards.quote: it is too bulky to pack into the small sphere, a micelle, that single-tailed soaps form
cards.section: What pays for order: the hydrophobic effect

cards.front: A mutation in a protein's core reduces the amount of nonpolar surface that gets buried when the protein folds. Using the hydrophobic effect, predict the effect on folding stability.
cards.back: Destabilizing. Less nonpolar surface is buried, so less water is freed, and the burial term that pays most of the folding bill shrinks.
cards.why: Rests on burial of nonpolar surface freeing water.
cards.quote: Water freed from about 4,800 Å² of nonpolar surface buried in the core
cards.section: What pays for order: the hydrophobic effect

cards.front: Relative to its pKa, when does an acidic group mostly hold its proton, mostly lose it, or sit half and half?
cards.back: Below the pKa it mostly holds its proton; above it, it mostly lets go; at the pKa, half and half.
cards.quote: Below a group's pKa, the group mostly holds its proton; above it, it mostly lets go; at the pKa, half and half.
cards.section: pH: the ledger for charge

cards.front: Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log({{c1::[A⁻]/[HA]}}), where HA is the protonated form.
cards.quote: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation writes the rule out: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
cards.section: pH: the ledger for charge

cards.front: A side-chain group has a pKa of 8.0. At pH 6.0, what is the ratio [A⁻]:[HA], and roughly what share is deprotonated?
cards.back: pH − pKa = −2, so [A⁻]/[HA] = 10⁻² = 1:100. About 1% is deprotonated; the group mostly holds its proton.
cards.quote: Call the protonated form HA and the form that has lost its proton A⁻.
cards.section: pH: the ledger for charge

cards.front: Glycine has a carboxyl group (pKa 2.3) and an amino group (pKa 9.6). What is its predominant form and net charge at pH 1.0?
cards.back: pH 1.0 is below both pKa values, so both groups mostly hold their protons: –COOH (neutral) and –NH₃⁺. Net charge about +1.
cards.quote: Glycine has a carboxyl group (pKa 2.3) and an amino group (pKa 9.6).
cards.section: pH: the ledger for charge

cards.front: Why does a simple buffer in a sealed flask work best within about one pH unit of its pKa?
cards.back: Far from the pKa one form has nearly run out, leaving little to absorb added acid or base.
cards.quote: Far from the pKa, one form has nearly run out, leaving little to absorb added acid or base
cards.section: pH: the ledger for charge

cards.front: What is the normal range of blood pH, and what is the effective pKa of the bicarbonate buffer that guards it?
cards.back: 7.35 to 7.45, a window one tenth of a pH unit wide. The bicarbonate buffer's effective pKa is 6.1.
cards.quote: Blood pH lives between 7.35 and 7.45, a window one tenth of a pH unit wide
cards.section: pH: the ledger for charge

cards.front: Blood is at pH 7.4 and the bicarbonate buffer's effective pKa is 6.1. What is the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved CO₂?
cards.back: log([HCO₃⁻]/[CO₂]) = 7.4 − 6.1 = 1.3, so the ratio is 10^1.3 ≈ 20:1.
cards.quote: At 7.4 that is 1.3 units off, about 20 bicarbonate ions per dissolved CO₂ (10^1.3 ≈ 20)
cards.section: pH: the ledger for charge

cards.front: The bicarbonate buffer sits 1.3 pH units from its pKa, a poor buffer by the sealed-flask rule. Why does it still protect blood pH so well?
cards.back: Blood is an open system: breathing carries extra CO₂ away, so the acid side of the ratio is held down while acid is added.
cards.why: In real blood, hemoglobin and other buffers also take up acid, and the kidneys restore bicarbonate.
cards.quote: It works because blood is not sealed: breathing carries the extra CO₂ away.
cards.section: pH: the ledger for charge

cards.front: In a bicarbonate-only model (24 mM HCO₃⁻, 1.2 mM CO₂, pKa 6.1), 10 mM strong acid is added, converting 10 mM HCO₃⁻ to CO₂. Find the pH in a sealed flask and if breathing holds CO₂ at 1.2 mM.
cards.quote: In a sealed flask the pH falls to about 6.2 (14 mM HCO₃⁻ against 11.2 mM CO₂)
cards.section: pH: the ledger for charge

cards.front: Starting at pH 7.4, a patient hyperventilates until blood CO₂ halves, with bicarbonate unchanged. Predict the new pH and name the disturbance.
cards.back: About 7.7, a respiratory alkalosis. CO₂ is the acid side of the ratio; halving it doubles [HCO₃⁻]/[CO₂], so pH rises by log 2 ≈ 0.3.
cards.quote: CO₂ is the acid side of the ratio, so halving it doubles [HCO₃⁻]/[CO₂], and pH rises by log 2, about 0.3.
cards.section: pH: the ledger for charge

cards.front: Starting at pH 7.4, a patient hypoventilates until blood CO₂ doubles, with bicarbonate unchanged. In the bicarbonate-only model, predict the pH, and why it matters for proteins.
cards.back: pH falls by log 2 ≈ 0.3, to about 7.1 in this model, well outside 7.35 to 7.45. Groups near their pKa change protonation, so proteins change their charges and work less well.
cards.why: Mirror of the hyperventilation case, combined with the pKa rule for charge.
cards.quote: Cross much past the window and proteins change their charges and work less well
cards.section: pH: the ledger for charge

cards.front: Why can some proteins unfold both when heated and when cooled from physiological temperature?
cards.back: Heat unfolds them because the chain's entropy term wins. Cold unfolds them because the hydrophobic effect weakens as temperature falls, owing to a positive ΔCp on exposing nonpolar surface.
cards.quote: heat unfolds a protein because the chain's entropy wins, and cold because the hydrophobic effect weakens
cards.section: How temperature changes the hydrophobic effect

cards.front: A negative ΔG of folding says the native state is favored. What does it not tell you?
cards.back: How fast the chain gets there, or whether it gets there without help. Some proteins need help to fold, and amyloid can be even more stable than the native form.
cards.why: Folding avoids a random search of shapes by running downhill on a funnel-shaped energy landscape.
cards.quote: Many proteins fit, but some need help to fold, and amyloid can be even more stable than the native form.
cards.section: Favored is not the same as fast
